items.title: I built a WebGPU multiplayer game with Claude Code and limited coding experience
items.why_it_matters: An indie developer built and shipped a real-time multiplayer WebGPU game using Claude Code with very little prior coding experience. It proves that you don't need to be an expert to ship complex interactive apps when you leverage Claude Code effectively. This week, you can open Claude Code in your terminal, describe a simple interactive feature you want to add to your AI-ingest tool, and let Claude scaffold and run the code for you without overthinking the implementation.

items.title: Show HN: The mentor setup I've run for months, now as a Claude Code plugin
items.why_it_matters: A developer packaged their custom "mentor" prompt system into a Claude Code plugin designed to keep the AI focused on shipping rather than over-complicating things. This is a direct antidote to your over-learning phase, helping you maintain momentum. This week, you can clone this repository and load the system prompt rules into your local Claude Code configuration to force the AI to keep your Next.js and Supabase code paths as simple and shippable as possible.

items.title: `bun init` automatically creates a Claude.md file by default
items.why_it_matters: Bun's initialization command now automatically generates a `Claude.md` file by default to provide instant context to Claude. This highlights a growing standard of keeping LLM-readable documentation directly inside your repository to make vibe coding faster. This week, you can manually create a `Claude.md` file in your AI-ingest root directory containing your Next.js + Supabase stack details so Claude Code instantly understands your project's architecture every time you start a session.

items.title: Show HN: Ctrlb-decompose: Strip the noise from logs before sending to LLMs
items.why_it_matters: This new CLI tool strips out the noise, timestamps, and redundant metadata from system logs before you send them to an LLM, dramatically reducing token usage and improving the AI's debugging accuracy. Since you rely on Claude Code to write and debug your code, this will save you money and get you cleaner fixes. This week, you can install this tool via npm and use it to clean up your Next.js build or Supabase error logs before passing them to Claude Code.

items.title: SessionRadar – Monitor Claude Code and Codex sessions from your menu bar
items.why_it_matters: SessionRadar is a new macOS menu bar utility designed specifically to monitor your active Claude Code and Codex sessions. It helps you keep track of your active terminal agent tasks and token spend at a glance so you don't run up unexpected API bills while vibe coding. This week, you can download the tool to monitor your local development sessions and keep your API costs transparent while building AI-ingest.

items.title: Claude Code system prompt says not to ask for permission, assumes user is absent
items.why_it_matters: An analysis of Claude Code's system prompt reveals that the tool is explicitly instructed to proceed with file edits without asking for permission, assuming the user is absent. Understanding this default behavior is key to mastering the "direction" part of vibe coding so you know when to step in. This week, you can add a custom instruction to your local `.clauderc` file telling Claude Code to always show a diff and ask for confirmation before writing changes to your Next.js files.
